senses: A Thai curry of Muslim origin (or the paste used to make it), usually containing coconut milk, roasted peanuts, potatoes, bay leaves, cardamom pods, cinnamon, palm sugar, fish sauce, and tamarind sauce.
ety: From Thai มัสมั่น (mát-sà-màn, “Muslim-like curry”), from Persian مسلمان (mosalmân, “Muslim”), from Arabic مُسْلِم (muslim, “Muslim”).

senses: Unable to be interpreted.
A power generation company.
ety: Short for generation company; compare pubco, telco.

senses: Allied by blood; kindred by birth; specifically (law) related on the mother's side.
Of the same or a similar nature; of the same family; proceeding from the same stock or root.
ety: Borrowed from Latin cognātus (“related by blood”), from co- + gnātus (“born”). Compare Portuguese cognato and Spanish cognado. Doublet of connate and cognatus.

senses: An old English measure of volume, perhaps equal to two bushels.
ety: Perhaps from Proto-West Germanic *metan (“to measure”). Cognate with German Metze.
examples: Once the mitta, or mett, a quantity of two bushels, is used for salt. The name still lingers in Lancashire.

senses: A traditional German cake eaten at Christmas time, made with nuts, raisins and other dried fruits.
ety: Borrowed from German Stollen. Doublet of stull.

senses: An inflatable suit to provide thermal insulation to the wearer and keep them dry while immersed in water.
A brown, fatty, waxy substance (fatty acids) that forms on dead animal tissues in response to hydrolysis.
a small, usually wooden drinking vessel
A harmful ghost believed to leave the body upon death and linger near the deceased's possessions.
That causes, or is associated with diarrhea.
A type of frame drum used in Irish music struck traditionally with an animal bone, or in modern times, with a piece of wood.
Someone who works with radiography. This term seems to be more common in British English.
The deliberate omission of something.
ety: From Latin ēlīsiō (“striking out, forcing out”) (whence -ion (“noun suffix denoting action, result, process, state, condition”)), from ēlīsus (“knocked out, forced out”), past participle of ēlīdō (“to knock, dash or strike out”) (whence elide), from ex- (“out, away”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence e- (“assimilated form of ex-”)).

senses: The inner layer of a spore.
A small vegetative spore produced by some bacteria.
A part of a serial issued from time to time.
A drained basin near a church's altar for the disposal of water from liturgical ablutions.
A basin or tank, especially one for holding fishes or for growing aquatic plants.
ety: From Latin piscīna (“fishpond; swimming pool”), from piscis (“fish”). Compare Middle English piscyne (“pool, pond”), from the same Latin word. By surface analysis, Latin pisc- + -ina.

senses: A text presented in six parallel versions, especially (historical) the version of the Old Testament presented in such a fashion by Origen.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἑξαπλᾶ (hexaplâ), neuter plural of ἑξαπλοῦς (hexaploûs, “sixfold”), from ἑξα- (hexa-, “hexa-: six”) + -πλόος (-plóos, “-fold”).

senses: A traditional Indian unit of measure for mass, approximately 0.1215 grams.
A Dutch liqueur made of egg yolks, sugar and strong liquor, typically brandy.
The act of trivializing.
A set of one or more steps surmounting a fence or wall, or a narrow gate or contrived passage through a fence or wall, which in either case allows people but not livestock to pass.
A vertical component of a frame or panel, such as that of a door, window, or ladder.
ety: From Middle English stile, style, stiȝele, from Old English stiġel (“stile, set of steps for getting over a fence”), from Proto-West Germanic *stigilu, from Proto-Germanic *stigilō (“entry, entrance, overpass, device for climbing, stile”), equivalent to sty (“to ascend, climb”) + -le. Cognate with Dutch stegel (“stirrup”), Low German Stegel (“stile”), German Stiegel (“stile”).

senses: Of medium size or extent; between microscale and macroscale.
Roughly 2–200 kilometers (or ~1-124 miles) in extent; between microscale and synoptic.
Between subbands.
nervy, jumpy, on edge
Having jitter, or unwanted signal characteristics.
A Turkish Angora cat.
A goat of a domesticated breed that produces mohair.

A rabbit belonging to the Angora rabbit breed, one of the oldest domestic breeds of rabbits in the world, raised chiefly in Europe for its silky and long hair (a subspecies of the European rabbit, Oryctolagus cuniculus).
The hair of angora rabbits or angora goats, used to make textiles.
The fabric made from the hair of angora rabbits or angora goats.
ety: From the name of the city of Ankara in Turkey, from Ancient Greek ἄγκυρα (ánkura, “anchor”).

senses: A female vampiric ghost in Malaysian and Indonesian mythology, said to be the spirit of a woman who died while pregnant.
examples: One of the most fearsome creatures of Malay folklore is the pontianak.

senses: Synonym of lusca; a shark-headed creature with tentacles; a Bahamian folkloric sea monster recast in U.S. pop culture pulp fiction
ety: Blend of shark + octopus, from being a half-shark/half-cephalopod sea monster

senses: A disturbance to an otherwise normal biological rhythm, especially that of the heart.
examples: Jet lag is also known as circadian dysrhythmia.

senses: Commonwealth standard spelling of encyclopedia.
ety: Borrowed from New Latin encyclopaedia; the English word is an etymologically restored spelling variant of earlier encyclopedia, q.v.

senses: A donkey or ass.
An idiot; a stupid or contemptible person.
ety: From Ned + -y, Ned being a diminutive of Edward.

senses: Something that restrains.
A heavy weatherproof jacket
Covered in pock marks; specifically, pox-ridden, syphilitic.
Possessing a stalk.
ety: From New Latin stīpitātus, from Classical Latin stīpes + -ātus. Compare stipe.

senses: A domestic spinning wheel, used mostly for spinning cotton.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani چرخہ (carxa) / चरख़ा (carxā), from Classical Persian چرخ (čarx), from Middle Persian 𐫝𐫍𐫡 (chr /⁠čahr⁠/, “wheel, cycle”), from Proto-Iranian *čaxrám, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *čakrám, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“wheel, circle”). Doublet of chakra, chakram, chukker, cycle, cyclus, kike, and wheel.

senses: A little bit.
examples: Keep Joss-house a litty on the larbourd-bow. Steady as you go.

I will send you some sweet cakes and a few light cakes and a litty buter, and a few apples and a pair of socks, and your litty girls wants to send you a sweet potato but I dont no if I can get them in my sack.
He dealt warily with traders, whom he classified in three groups: "'He cheat a litty" — "He cheat plenty" — and "I think he cheat too much.'"

senses: A stepfather.
An Italian relish made of pickled vegetables.
ety: From Italian giardiniera. Doublet of jardinière.
examples: The cheeses I’d laid out oozed invitation. As planned, the tang of my accompanying giardiniera nudged guests toward the tannic relief of drink.

senses: The study of landforms, their classification, origin, development, and history.
